articles.title: Washington voters protected women’s sports. ACLU wants to overturn democracy
articles.summary: Washington state voters passed Initiative 638 to protect women's sports, but the ACLU's lawsuit now threatens to overturn their more than 10-point margin.
articles.body: I ran a lot of track for many years. I’m fast enough that, back in high school, I was named Female Track & Field Athlete of the Year three years in a row by my school’s coaching staff. But I’m not a male. Male athletes have strength and speed I’ll never have, and when I step out on the track, forced to run against one, I know, before the pistol even fires, that the result is already decided—we’re just going through the motions. Voters in four states—red and blue—understood this when they went to the ballot box on Nov. 3 and passed measures protecting women's sports. Now the American Civil Liberties Union is seeking to undo the one in Washington state. Other female athletes and I won’t take this without a fight, because we speak from experience. In one of my best high school events—the girls' 4x400-meter relay race—my relay team ran against a male athlete who had previously competed in the high school boys' category. He beat us, easily, and went on to beat a lot of other girls. He even won the state championship in the women’s 400-meter race two years in a row. ACLU OF WASHINGTON SAYS IT WILL SUE TO BLOCK BALLOT INITIATIVE TO PROTECT GIRLS' SPORTS No female athlete runs to lose, any more than a male does. We didn’t put ourselves through all that rigorous training, grind through those straining workouts or run those endless sprints for the fun of watching someone else finish race after race ahead of us. When males enter girls’ sports, that’s not competition. Running races you’re guaranteed to win is not competition; neither is entering races you’re guaranteed to lose. All these male athletes are doing is securing automatic trophies for themselves while women like me lose roster spots, records, medals, our turn on the podium, and our privacy. Voters had to do that; our legislators wouldn’t. But then, our voters understand what our elected representatives can’t seem to grasp: that biology isn’t red or blue. WASHINGTON AG'S OFFICE INDICATES IT WILL DEFEND GIRLS' SPORTS BALLOT MEASURE AFTER ACLU SUES TO BLOCK IT Years ago, Congress passed Title IX to ensure that wouldn’t happen. Earlier this month, seeing that social and political movements had combined to undercut that landmark law, Washington state voters, Democrats and Republicans alike, rallied to pass Initiative 638—by a margin of more than 10 percentage points—to vindicate Title IX and protect women's sports. Voters had to do that; our legislators wouldn’t. But then, our voters understand what our elected representatives can’t seem to grasp: that biology isn’t red or blue. This is not a partisan issue—it’s common sense. And it’s up to the state of Washington to defend in court what a clear majority of its citizens have made law at the ballot box. WASHINGTON PARENTS FIND THEIR COURAGE AS GIRLS WALK OFF CROSS COUNTRY COURSE IN PROTEST OF TRANS RUNNER We need our officials to step up, because the ACLU—unable to make its case that men should be in women’s sports at the ballot box—is demanding that a state court go around us and overturn Initiative 638. To ensure the ACLU doesn't succeed, Alliance Defending Freedom is representing Female Athletes United, a coalition of female athletes, in filing a motion to intervene in the ACLU’s lawsuit. I’m filing a declaration as part of that lawsuit. I’ve been here before. Last year, I filed a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights, asking it to investigate our state’s athletic policies and require that sex-designated sports categories be based on sex. I did that not only for myself but for countless other young women across my state who’ve been on the receiving end of this issue for years—and for our younger sisters, waiting to take their own blows for the cause. This isn’t about wounded pride. It’s about safety: another female athlete in our state, Kallie Keeler, for instance, suffered great harm during a high school women’s wrestling match against a competitor who turned out to be male. None of the coaches or officials had bothered to tell her. It’s also about privacy: Would you want your daughter changing clothes and showering with men who’ve politicized their way into her locker room? And it’s about fairness. A United Nations report documents more than 600 female athletes across 29 sports who’ve been displaced by men; the men collectively took more than 890 medals. But then, just in West Virginia, one male defeated more than 470 girls over 1,400 times in a single sport. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION That’s the instance that resulted in last summer’s State of West Virginia v. B.P.J. case, in which the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that states can protect women’s sports. Twenty-seven states have passed legislation to do just that; in this month’s midterm elections, voters in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington joined them. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Now we know where the public stands on this issue. We hope the state officials who failed us once are going to step up this time to stand with us. But we’re not waiting to find out.

articles.title: Girls as young as five targeted for upskirting as charges continue to rise
articles.summary: Police forces have received complaints involving girls as young as five and women as old as 87.
articles.body:
Girls as young as five have been targeted for upskirting, new police figures show.

Over the past three years, Wales' four forces received 219 complaints from females up to the age of 87, with 18 people charged, results of Freedom of Information (FOI) requests reveal.

Upskirting involves taking a photo or video beneath someone's clothing - without their knowledge - with the intention of viewing their genitals, buttocks or underwear.

It was made a criminal offence under the Voyeurism (Offences) Act 2019 and carries a maximum sentence of two years in prison.

The Crown Prosecution Service urged people to report incidents immediately, saying those that led to charges almost doubled between 2022 and 2026.

"As well as being an extremely damaging offence in its own right, our prosecutors often see upskirting forming part of a wider pattern of sexual offending," said national lead for sexual offence prosecutions Siobhan Blake.

Between January 2023 and June 2026, Wales' four police forces received 219 complaints, with the highest being 159 in the Dyfed-Powys area and the lowest, six in Gwent, according to the FOI figures.

Where ages were recorded, 11 involved under-10s, 67 came from girls aged 11 to 17, 35 from those 18 to 24, and 12 from over-55s.

From these 219 complaints, nine people were charged in the north Wales force area, six in Dyfed-Powys, three in south Wales, while Gwent had no data.

A previous FOI to Greater Manchester Police showed it received 146 reports between 2019 and 2025, leading to 41 arrests and 10 people being charged.

West Midlands Police received 75 reports between 2022 and 2026, with 23 charged, according to another FOI .

"I think a lot of the time [boys] think it's a joke or banter, but it's not funny," said student Rowan Stanger, 21.

"Whilst it is illegal, I don't think a lot of people take it seriously."

She was in secondary school when it was made a criminal offence in Wales and England in 2019 , and as a teenager, heard about lots of cases of it happening to friends.

"I was wearing shorts under skirts in school, I think that's what was kind of expected even before I really knew why," she added.

"That is still ingrained in me. I'll rarely wear one without."

Rowan is part of a student-led Time to Act, which fights against sexual violence in higher education.

Emily Hasling, 23, is also part of the Cardiff-based campaign group, and said she remembers when she was in university and going to nightclubs, she would only wear jeans.

"Young boys don't see it as sexual assault or sexual violence, because it's not a physical kind of touching element, it's a photo," she said.

"So that's how they see it 'just a photo'."

Another group member Freya Price, 22, described feeling wary on public transport.

"Obviously trains are quite crowded so if I can't stand in a corner I'll feel quite anxious, because I can't guarantee that someone's not going to violate my privacy," she said.

In September 2020, Dominique Pelicot was caught after a supermarket security guard saw him filming under women's skirts.

It prompted a police search of his electronic devices, which uncovered thousands of files revealing a decade-long scheme to drug and sexually abuse his wife, Gisele.

A former North Wales Police detective is also due to be sentenced later this year after admitting taking pictures beneath the clothing of a child without consent.

Lee Harshey-Jones, 45, was a detective constable and lead investigator in the case of two-year-old Ethan Ives-Griffiths, whose grandparents were jailed for murder last year, and has given evidence in other high-profile murder trials in north Wales.

He pleaded guilty to one charge of voyeurism and one of perverting the course of justice by applying a factory reset to his mobile phone to conceal evidence.

Last month a former supply teacher was jailed for six years after taking more than 100 upskirt photographs of schoolgirls, including in his classroom, across Greater Manchester.

Recently the operator of the popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest took proactive measures and handed out free cycling shorts to women , after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.

Olivia (not her real name), a teenager from south Wales, said she loves wearing skirts but from an early age has been made to feel uncomfortable in them.

She described how boys in primary school had an obsession with "flipping up girls' skirts", which led to them either wearing shorts underneath or switching to trousers.

This was her first experience of feeling unsafe in them, while she was then upskirted on a night out while at university.

"There was a little stage area and I'm dancing, having a great time," Olivia said.

"I look over to my right and someone has got a camera with the flash on underneath my skirt.

"We made eye contact and he walked off. I was frozen and I didn't know if I was imagining it. I didn't know if I could tell someone or who to tell."

She has not felt comfortable enough to wear the same dress again until recently, describing her head as being "on a swivel" every time she was in a club, and feeling like she could not get too drunk.

In 2019, Libby Squire, 21, was raped and murdered by Pawel Relowicz, who was found to have previous convictions for voyeurism and public sex acts.

Libby's mother Lisa Squire has spent the past five years trying to increase the reporting of non-contact sexual offences, launching the It Does Matter campaign in 2024.

"I know first hand how harmful behaviours that are too often dismissed as 'minor' can build into something catastrophic, and I am committed to ensuring no other family experiences what we have," she said.

The NSPCC said its Childline service has heard from young people who have had indecent images of them taken and shared.

"They tell us how devastating the abuse can be on their mental and emotional wellbeing, leaving them afraid, ashamed and unsure where to turn," a spokesperson said.

One 16-year-old described how the same boy tripped her up on the way to her seat every day in her tutor group, laughing and looking up her skirt.

"It just freaks me out and I don't know what to do about it," she said.

A mum called to say her daughter, also 16, had heard a rumour a boy in her year had taken a photograph up her skirt, and shared it with his friends.

She added: "The thought alone is incredibly upsetting for her."

The Children's Commissioner for England said Children's Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza said: "The fact a number of teachers have admitted or been found guilty of upskirting offences , some in their own classrooms, is particularly shocking.

"Teachers and other school professionals have a clear responsibility to keep children safe, so staff must be alert to the signs of sexual harassment and abuse and ensure all children know where they can turn for help and support if an incident occurs."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC Action Line

articles.title: Iraqi forces strike compromise with powerful pro-Iran militia, security officials say
articles.summary: BAGHDAD, Iraq — Iraq has reached a compromise with the powerful Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah, three senior security officials said, after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group.
articles.body: BAGHDAD, Iraq — Iraq has reached a compromise with the powerful Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah, three senior security officials said, after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readied security forces to move against the group. Iraqi officials had accused the group of running a smuggling ring that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of state-owned oil. Under the deal brokered by senior Shi’ite political leaders to avert a confrontation, government forces were expected to move into the group’s stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday, according to three security officials familiar with the deal. Kataib forces would move to other areas, Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq’s Security Media Cell, told Reuters. Reflecting the gravity of the situation, Iraqi Shi’ite political sources said Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s elite Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad late on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataib Hezbollah, Tehran’s most powerful militia ally in Iraq. A spokesperson for Kataib Hezbollah said the group’s secretary-general, Abu Hussein al-Hamidawi, met Qaani, Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization, another influential Iran-aligned militia, and other influential figures in a bid to prevent an escalation. Participants described the outcome of the talks as positive in a statement issued on Thursday. Risky move Zaidi, a political novice, has made his riskiest move since he came to power six months ago by directly confronting the heavily armed Shi’ite militias that function as proxies of Iran. Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib Hezbollah, have resisted calls by Zaidi and US President Donald Trump to disarm. These groups enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. Kataib and other militias say they are dedicated to Iraq’s security. They have attacked US troops in solidarity with Iran since the United States and Israel launched a war against the Islamic Republic in February. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God) has thousands of hardened fighters. It forms several battalions in Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces, a grouping of armed factions originally set up to fight Islamic State in 2014 that was subsequently recognized as an official security force. While it is technically under the command of Iraq’s prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates outside the chain of command and has defied and challenged government statements calling for an end to attacks on US forces. Founded in the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, Kataib Hezbollah is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, the umbrella group of hardline Shi’ite armed organizations supported by Iran. Like other Shi’ite armed groups, Kataib Hezbollah reports directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. It was led by dual Iraqi-Iranian citizen Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis until he was killed in a US drone strike in 2020 along with the commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, Qassem Soleimani, at Baghdad’s international airport.

articles.title: Six killed in suspected gas explosion at Georgia apartment building
articles.summary: Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili said rescuers had recovered six bodies from the wreckage.
articles.body:
Six people, including a child, have been killed after a suspected natural gas explosion caused part of a five-storey apartment building to collapse in Georgia’s capital, Tbilisi, according to the AFP news agency.

The blast struck the residential building in the suburban Ponichala district on Thursday morning, trapping several residents beneath the rubble.

Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili said rescuers had recovered six bodies from the wreckage, including that of a young child.

A three-year-old girl was pulled alive from the rubble after several hours of rescue operations, prompting applause from onlookers gathered at the scene.

Emergency Management Service chief Teimuraz Mgebrishvili said one of the women found dead was believed to be the girl’s mother, according to AFP.

Doctors at Ingorokva University Clinic said the rescued girl was in stable condition and scans had revealed no serious traumatic injuries, Georgian Public Broadcaster (1TV) reported.

An 11-year-old boy was also being treated in intensive care, although his condition was described as relatively stable, according to the broadcaster.

Tamazashvili said preliminary findings indicated that the explosion occurred on the fifth floor when a resident attempted to switch on a gas heater.

However, gas supplier Tbilisi Energy said the apartment identified as the likely source of the explosion had been registered as unoccupied and had recorded no gas consumption over the past year, according to 1TV. The company said it had not yet been able to inspect the damaged property.

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said authorities would temporarily relocate 28 families, comprising more than 100 residents, to hotels after structural assessments found two sections of the building unsafe, according to Georgia’s Interpressnews agency.

Prosecutor Levan Vepkhvadze said a criminal investigation had been launched into possible violations of safety regulations.

articles.title: Pakistan military says it killed 22 militants in raids on hideouts in northwest
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD — Pakistani security forces acting on intelligence raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants, the military said Thursday.
articles.body: ISLAMABAD — Pakistani security forces acting on intelligence raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants, the military said Thursday. It alleged that the militants killed were backed by neighboring India. There was no immediate comment from New Delhi, but Pakistan often accuses Afghanistan and India of supporting the Pakistani Taliban and other militant groups, allegations both countries deny. The raids took place over the past 48 hours in the South Waziristan, Bannu and Tank districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the military said in a statement. The military reported last week that security forces had killed 74 militants over several days in raids on hideouts in the northwest and in southwestern Balochistan province. The military said troops were searching the areas for any remaining militants and pledged to continue operations against what it described as foreign-backed terrorism. President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in separate statements praised the security forces for eliminating “Indian-supported” militants and vowed to continue the fight against militancy. Sharif said militants and their supporters would not be allowed to spread unrest in Pakistan and that the nation stood behind the forces fighting them. Militant attacks targeting Pakistan’s police and security forces have surged in recent years. Authorities have blamed the Pakistani Taliban, who are known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan or TTP, and allied militant groups for most of the violence. The Pakistani Taliban are a separate group from but allied with Afghanistan’s Taliban, who took power in Kabul in 2021. Many TTP leaders and fighters are believed to operate from sanctuaries across the Afghan border, straining relations between Islamabad and Kabul.

articles.title: Zelenskyy presses US for expanded Russia talks as Kushner announces breakthrough
articles.summary: Jared Kushner said Russia agreed to multilateral Ukraine war talks involving Europe after Zelenskyy urged the Trump administration to move quickly.
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling on the U.S. to quickly organize talks with Russia with the full participation of European negotiators and advisors in what would mark a first-of-its-kind meeting. He made the call Thursday after meeting with several U.S. and European leaders in Berlin at the Coalition of the Willing summit, which focused on security guarantees aimed at deterring future Russian aggression. During the meeting, U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner announced that Moscow and President Donald Trump had agreed to a multilateral negotiating format involving Europe. "We are counting on the American side to help organize the first multilateral meeting at the team level, with full European participation, as soon as possible," Zelenskyy said. The push signals an effort to prevent Europe and Kyiv from being sidelined in U.S.-Russia talks. KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE "From the very beginning, Ukraine has advocated for this approach — maximum coordination among us on everything concerning European and Ukrainian security and our future," Zelenskyy said. "We need to work quickly, and this is the only approach Ukraine is taking. The more actively the discussions move forward, the greater the chances of achieving real progress." According to Kushner, Russia agreed to the expanded negotiating format, including a recent breakthrough on prisoner exchanges. "Russia has agreed to engage in the multilateral format with the Europeans. Part of that was us explaining to the Russians that we do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential to ending this war in a just and long-term, durable way," Kushner said. "There's going to be thousands of prisoners of war who will be going home to their families in the next weeks, which will be, obviously, a great gesture and a great relief for people." FRENCH TROOPS SECRETLY DEPLOYED INSIDE UKRAINE AS EX-NATO CHIEF PRAISES MACRON'S 'GUTS' He added that President Donald Trump will not impose a unilateral deal but will work with allies to finalize postwar security guarantees. "President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He's not looking to impose anything unilaterally," Kushner said. articles.title: Locals of Michigan city with largest Muslim population believe America should look more like Dearborn
articles.summary: Dearborn locals celebrate their city's diversity as Warren, Michigan residents worry about being pushed out as Muslim immigrants reshape their hometown.
articles.body: Residents of Dearborn, Michigan, a city with one of the nation's largest Muslim populations, told Fox News Digital that other cities should embrace diversity instead of fearing becoming "the next Dearborn." "I hear intolerance when I hear something like that. I hear communities that don't understand what they're missing out on. They're missing out on culture," Diedo told Fox News Digital. "They're missing out on awareness. I went to Dearborn Divine Child for high school, for grade school, for middle school – people that say that they are unfamiliar with what's coming and what's coming is going to be great y'all, so stand by for it," he added. ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE Jamal Jawad, owner of The Custard Company, told Fox News Digital that diversity is beneficial to the country. "It's good to be diverse. You have people of different faiths, people of different cultures all over the place, all over the country. I mean it's good," Jawad said inside Toum, a new restaurant he was preparing to open in western Dearborn. The nearby city of Warren, Michigan, another Detroit suburb, has also experienced demographic changes. The sale of a local church for conversion into the Al Ihsaan Islamic Center reflects one such change. In Warren, several residents interviewed by Fox News Digital said they felt like they're being pushed out of their own hometown as Muslims immigrate to the area, expressing concerns about being the "next Dearborn." Warren, Michigan's third-largest city after Detroit and Grand Rapids, grew rapidly during the post-World War II auto manufacturing boom, as war veterans moved to the area to work for Ford and General Motors. The blue-collar, white-picket-fence community incorporated as a city in 1957. NYC'S MAMDANI SAYS ABDUL EL-SAYED'S SENATE VICTORY IN MICHIGAN 'MEANS SO MUCH TO SO MANY' Dearborn residents embraced Muslim and Arab immigration to Michigan and rejected warnings about the area's changing demographics. "That's bad. Come on, we gotta get past all that stuff," Dave Tilbot told Fox News Digital. Another Dearborn resident, who did not disclose his name, said: "That is not an insult, it's actually a great thing, because I feel like the rest of America should be a little similar to Dearborn because it's a city, a beautiful city full of lots of people and all types of people: Mexican, Asian, Chinese, Arabic, American, Blacks." "We got all types of people around here and it's a beautiful, beautiful city so I hope the world could become like Dearborn," he added. JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS Ahmad Seif, a graduate of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor who makes sushi for a living, told Fox News Digital that Dearborn is home to people from a variety of Arab backgrounds. "I think ‘the next Dearborn’ is a big statement because there's never going to be a place like Dearborn where there's so many Arabs in one place … maybe like New York, but even then it's like Dearborn has so much different kinds of Arabs too," Seif said. He added, "It's not just one kind like we have Yemenis, we have Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian, Iraqis …" Immigrants from Lebanon, Iraq and Syria began settling in the Detroit area in the early 20th century, drawn in part by growing demand for labor in the auto industry. DEARBORN SCHOOLS APOLOGIZE AFTER 200-PLUS STUDENTS MISTAKENLY SERVED PORK DURING RAMADAN Hala, a Dearborn resident, told Fox News Digital that Dearborn has the best food. "I think that's the best compliment we could be ‘the next Dearborn’ who doesn't wanna be in Dearborn?" she asked. Deronda Evans, an educator, told Fox News Digital that she views the prospect of another city becoming the "next Dearborn" positively. "I hear something positive because Dearborn is developing and it's really multicultural. They have some good things going on, and some abandoned buildings are now businesses and have good choices, have good vibes, and I feel safe when I'm here," Evans said. She went on to say, "I come here very often just to chill and enjoy myself, so I hear something positive because it's developing just like Detroit is developing." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed delivered a victory speech at an Arab America Foundation summit in Virginia shortly after Election Day, where he called Michigan the "capital of Arab America." "I know we’re here in D.C., which, of course, is the capital of the United States of America. But Michigan is the capital of Arab America," El-Sayed said. Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud told Fox News Digital this week what he thought El-Sayed meant by that statement. articles.title: Lahori Zeera, Campa Jeera: Cumin-laced fizzy sodas are giving the cola giants a tough fight in India
articles.summary: Cumin-laced sodas are capturing a bigger market share in India as demand for homegrown flavours goes up.
articles.body:
It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.

Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.

They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.

Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.

The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.

Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; £0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.

Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.

Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.

There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.

Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.

"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."

Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.

Parle Agro , one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.

Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.

The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.

According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.

"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.

"In global markets, established duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; an 8% swing in less than a year is a structural disruption."

Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".

For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.

With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.

But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.

Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.

Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.

This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.

"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.

The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.

While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.

Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.

Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.

"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.

Coca Cola, which had acquired the cumin-flavoured Rimzim brand in the 1990s, is strengthening its play in this category and reportedly doubled production last year.

But the challenges haven't deterred the ambitions of the homegrown players.

"Indian flavours need to find a global spotlight," says Munjal, who is looking to tap the global market in the coming years.

"For generations, we've grown up drinking colas of the world, but I hope the next generations will drink the zeeras of India."

articles.title: Teen accused of fatally shooting identical twin brother after fight about touching his belongings
articles.summary: Jamari Young, 16, was arrested in the Washington, D.C., shooting death of his identical twin brother, Jabrell Young. U.S. Marshals took Jamari into custody.
articles.body: A teenage boy was arrested Wednesday in the fatal shooting of his identical twin brother inside their Washington, D.C., home after an argument, police said. The U.S. Marshals Service took 16-year-old Jamari Young into custody, according to the Metropolitan Police Department. He was charged as an adult with second-degree murder while armed. On Thursday, a judge ordered the teen held without bond. Family members told affiliate FOX 5 DC they turned Young in to authorities after the Oct. 25 death of his brother, Jabrell Young, also 16. TEEN ARRESTED IN GIRL'S MURDER ONE YEAR AFTER POLICE SAID SHE ACCIDENTALLY SHOT HERSELF WHILE RECORDING VIDEO Officers responding to the home that day found Jabrell unconscious and not breathing. He was pronounced dead inside the home, where he died in his mother's arms, relatives said. Prior to the shooting, the brothers had been in an argument over Jabrell going into Jamari's room and touching his belongings, according to court documents obtained by the news outlet. As the boys' mother applied pressure to Jabrell's wounds in an effort to save his life, Jamari allegedly said, "I didn’t mean to. It just went off. I didn’t mean to. I’m sorry, Ma." The twins' mother allegedly yelled at her son to leave the house after the shooting. Neighborhood security cameras showed Jamari walking and then running from the neighborhood. Detectives investigated the death as a homicide, and a search for Jamari was launched. Authorities found two .45-caliber shell casings inside the house but have yet to recover the weapon used in the killing. GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS After the shooting, someone in the home allegedly tossed a blanket under a nearby parked car, where officers found a 9 mm pistol inside that was traced to an unsolved fatal shooting in July, FOX 5 reported. Authorities have not confirmed who tossed the blanket under the parked car. Investigators also have not disclosed where Jamari went after leaving the residence or whether he was given assistance while missing. The twins' aunt told the news outlet that the shooting was accidental, saying Jamari was terrified and had not intended to shoot his brother. After Thursday's court hearing, the boys' mother said her sons were inseparable and that the shooting was an accident. TEEN ARRESTED ON MURDER CHARGES AFTER CITADEL CADET AND CHILDHOOD FRIEND FOUND SHOT DEAD "This is an accident. This is an accident, but they're putting out a narrative that my son is just a monster and that this is something that was just malicious," she told FOX 5. "This is not malicious, sir. My son and his brother are best friends. They love each other. Ride or die." She added that she feels her family has been targeted by law enforcement. "I've been harassed. I've been stalked. I've been threatened. I've been mistreated. My family has been mistreated since day one," she said. "I've been treated like I'm the suspect. I haven't been treated like I'm a grieving mom. I've been treated like I'm the one whose [at] fault for all this." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In an online fundraiser, the twins' mother said Jamari was "being portrayed in a way that could put his life in danger." She said investigators took all of her electronic devices and that "i continue to face legal pressure while i am still trying to grieve and find the strength to get through each day," according to the fundraiser, which had raised more than $1,200 for the family as of Thursday afternoon.

articles.title: Muçulmanos serão maioria religiosa no mundo até 2035, diz estudo | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa divulgada pela Pew Research Center sobre o futuro das religiões no mundo aponta que as duas religiões estão em crescimento, mas ritmo é maior com muçulmanos.
articles.summary: Um estudo da Pew Research Center revela que o número de muçulmanos cresce em ritmo acelerado e deve ultrapassar o de cristãos devido a tendências demográficas globais.
articles.body:
Um homem muçulmano reza na mesquita Dawatagaha Jumma Masjid durante as orações do meio-dia de sexta-feira em Colombo, no Sri Lanka, onde uma série de explosões em igrejas e hotéis de luxo deixou centenas de mortos no domingo (21) durante a celebração da Páscoa — Foto: Ishara S. Kodikara/AFP

Muçulmanos vão passar os cristãos para se tornarem o maior grupo religioso do mundo até 2035. É o que indica pesquisa divulgada pela Pew Research Center sobre o futuro das religiões no mundo.

Segundo o estudo, há um crescimento dos dois grupos religiosos ao mesmo tempo, mas com maior velocidade com os muçulmanos. Hoje, o estudo registrou 2,27 bilhões de cristãos e 2,02 bilhões de muçulmanos.

A tendência, se a curva mantiver no atual cenário, é de termos mais de 3,6 bilhões de integrantes da religião até 2070, enquanto os cristãos ficarão perto de atingir 3 bilhões.

O ponto de virada ocorreria em 2035, segundo as previsões, quando os muçulmanos chegarão a 2,57 bilhões na população mundial e os cristãos, 2,52 bilhões.

Por séculos, o cristianismo tem sido a maior religião do mundo e representava 29% da população, em 2020. Muçulmanos eram 25,6%; religiões indefinidas, 24,2%; e hindus, 14,9%.

As previsões para 2027 indicam que os muçulmanos devem atingir 35,8% do mundo, enquanto o cristianismo fica estável, com 29,1%. Religiões indefinidas caem para 17%, já os hindus devem passar a representar 13,6%.

De acordo com o estudo, o crescimento mais acentuado no número de muçulmanos está diretamente relacionado a tendências demográficas nos países e regiões em que o grupo está em crescimento, como na África.

A previsão para o século 21 é de que o maior crescimento populacional ocorra no continente, em especial ao sul do Deserto do Saara.

A expectativa é de que mais de um quarto de todas as pessoas do mundo vivam na África subsaariana, que tem muçulmanos e cristãos como principais representantes de religiões em seus territórios.

articles.title: Dia da Consciência Negra: como a luta na ditadura virou feriado | G1
articles.standfirst: Antônio Carlos Côrtes, um dos idealizadores da data, afirma que o feriado nacional representa uma conquista histórica, mas diz que desafios que motivaram o movimento nos anos 1970 seguem presentes.
articles.summary: Um dos fundadores do Grupo Palmares revela como o Dia da Consciência Negra nasceu em reuniões secretas e se tornou um feriado nacional de reflexão e resistência.
articles.body:
Quando o Dia da Consciência Negra se tornou feriado nacional, Antônio Carlos Côrtes teve a confirmação de que uma ideia nascida entre um pequeno grupo de jovens negros no Rio Grande do Sul em 1971 havia ultrapassado governos e gerações.

Aos 77 anos, o advogado, escritor e um dos fundadores do Grupo Palmares afirma que o reconhecimento nacional do 20 de novembro foi o ponto mais alto de uma caminhada iniciada ainda durante a ditadura militar .

"Hoje, o 20 de novembro sendo feriado nacional, não feriado pelo feriado, mas uma data de reflexão em todo o país, não é pouca coisa. Eu penso que é o momento maior da coroação e dedico este momento à memória dos meus colegas fundadores", afirma.

🔎A data rememora a morte de Zumbi dos Palmares, líder do maior quilombo do Brasil no período colonial, assassinado em 1695, e foi proposta por um grupo de estudiosos e ativistas gaúchos como alternativa à celebração da Abolição da Escravatura, em 13 de maio.

🔎O Grupo Palmares nasceu durante a ditadura militar no Brasil, período de 1964 a 1985 em que houve repressão e censura da oposição ao governo, principalmente de artistas, escritores e imprensa.

Integrantes do Grupo Palmares duante congresso do movimento negro — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Formado por jovens estudantes negros do Rio Grande do Sul em 1971, o grupo Palmares mobilizava a luta antirracista e propôs o dia da morte de Zumbi dos Palmares como marco .

As reuniões dos jovens aconteciam sob o peso da repressão política e da censura, em um contexto em que reivindicar direitos ou questionar narrativas estabelecidas exigia articulação e persistência.

"Nos reuníamos em casas ou na Esquina Democrática, em Porto Alegre . Ali debatíamos democracia e políticas públicas para a população negra, que já habitava 85% da periferia da cidade", afirma Côrtes.

Mais do que organizar discussões sobre racismo, o Grupo Palmares buscava ampliar a presença da população negra no debate público. Os integrantes discutiam democracia, educação, cultura e memória histórica .

Ao recordar aqueles anos, Côrtes revela um detalhe pouco conhecido sobre a organização interna do movimento: embora o grupo fosse composto por seis pessoas, apenas quatro apareciam publicamente . Os outros dois permaneciam em segundo plano.

Além de Cortês, eram eles: Oliveira Silveira, Ilmo Silva, Vilmar Nunes, José Antônio dos Santos e Luiz Paulo Assis Santos — sendo esses dois últimos os integrantes "ocultos" do grupo.

A estratégia tinha uma razão simples: garantir a sobrevivência da iniciativa caso os integrantes mais expostos fossem perseguidos .

"Na realidade nós éramos seis, mas dois ficaram ocultos. Se a ditadura eliminasse aqueles quatro que botavam a cara para bater, os outros dois dariam sequência àquela célula", conta.

Décadas depois, Côrtes diz enxergar sua função quase como a de um guardião dessa memória. Dos integrantes do grupo, ele afirma ser o único que permaneceu vivendo no Rio Grande do Sul. Outros companheiros morreram ao longo do caminho.

Uma conquista construída ao longo de décadas

Embora a sanção do feriado nacional tenha ocorrido apenas em 2023 , Côrtes afirma que o caminho começou a ser pavimentado muito antes.

A origem da proposta remonta a uma descoberta feita por Côrtes na Biblioteca Pública do Estado, em Porto Alegre . Ao pesquisar a trajetória de Zumbi dos Palmares no livro O Quilombo dos Palmares, de Edison Carneiro, ele encontrou a data da morte do líder quilombola.

"Não descobri ( o dia do nascimento ), mas descobri a data da sua morte: 20 de novembro de 1695, na região onde hoje é Alagoas", relembra.

A informação foi levada aos demais integrantes do Grupo Palmares, que passaram a defender o 20 de novembro como referência para a luta da população negra em contraposição ao 13 de maio , data da celebração da Abolição da Escravatura.

Foi então que a proposta começou a circular entre organizações e lideranças do movimento negro em diferentes regiões do país, ampliando gradualmente o alcance da discussão até que o 20 de novembro se consolidasse como uma referência nacional.

Para o ativista, a transformação do 20 de novembro em feriado nacional não pode ser atribuída a uma única liderança nem a um único grupo.

"Fico em paz com a minha consciência, mas fico triste quando personalizam tudo. Não foi o Côrtes que fez isso. Foi um coletivo. O Grupo Palmares era um coletivo", reforça.

Segundo ele, justamente por ter sido construída de forma coletiva, a conquista adquiriu dimensão nacional.

"Não é fácil um país do tamanho do Brasil mobilizar-se para transformar uma data em patrimônio de todo o povo", confessa.

Côrtes vê a data de 20 de novembro como uma vitória histórica . A luta que o inspirou, porém, continua sendo assunto do presente.

Para ele, é uma oportunidade para que o país discuta desigualdades, políticas públicas e os desafios ainda existentes .

"O 20 de novembro tem um lado de reflexão. É um momento para discutir o que precisa ser melhorado, o que pode ser aperfeiçoado nas ações afirmativas e quais avanços ainda precisamos conquistar", pontua.

Na avaliação do ativista, a data também pode fortalecer o ensino da história africana e da população negra brasileira nas escolas:

"O negro está presente em todos os espaços culturais do país. Por isso, essa discussão precisa atravessar todas as disciplinas, da literatura à geografia, da história às artes."

Zumbi dos Palmares, líder do quilombo dos Palmares. — Foto: Reprodução

Ao falar sobre Zumbi dos Palmares, Côrtes destaca que o líder quilombola segue como símbolo de resistência e liberdade para a população negra . Na avaliação dele, a trajetória de Zumbi ajuda a compreender a luta contra a escravidão e a importância da preservação da memória histórica no Brasil.

Segundo Côrtes, Zumbi simboliza resistência, consciência de identidade e a construção de alternativas coletivas diante da opressão .

"Assim como o Brasil destaca Tiradentes como alguém que lutou pela liberdade, eu vejo Zumbi nesse mesmo patamar de importância histórica", destaca.

Para ele, o líder de Palmares continua relevante porque permite que novas gerações conheçam uma parte da história que, durante muito tempo, recebeu pouca atenção.

Ao analisar as transformações ocorridas nas últimas cinco décadas, Côrtes aponta as ações afirmativas e o sistema de cotas entre os principais avanços.

Para ele, essas políticas ajudaram a enfrentar desigualdades históricas e abriram caminhos para que mais negros chegassem às universidades e a espaços antes inacessíveis :

"As cotas vieram para ficar. Elas provaram seu valor. Os estudantes entram pelas cotas, mas não saem pelas cotas. Precisam demonstrar capacidade, dedicação e talento durante toda a trajetória acadêmica."

Ele também avalia que houve mudanças importantes na legislação relacionada ao racismo. Na juventude de sua geração, conta que não existiam instrumentos legais capazes de oferecer proteção efetiva às vítimas.

"O racismo era tratado quase como se fosse uma contravenção. Não existia o amparo que existe hoje. Havia preconceito, segregação e discriminação de forma muito mais aberta", revela.

Na sua visão, a existência de leis mais rigorosas não resolveu o problema, mas criou mecanismos para enfrentá-lo.

"Não significa que tudo está equilibrado, mas representa um avanço importante no nível de consciência da sociedade", afirma.

Antônio Carlos Cortês, 77 anos, advogado, escritor e um dos fundadores do Grupo Palmares — Foto: Anselmo Cunha/ Agencia RBS

Apesar dos avanços, a maior decepção de Côrtes é perceber que os problemas sociais enfrentados pela população negra ainda permanecem concentrados nos mesmos territórios .

Para ele, basta observar a realidade das periferias brasileiras para perceber que o país continua devendo respostas importantes:

"Quando olho as grandes cidades, vejo que a maioria negra e pobre continua nas periferias. Muitas vezes sem estrutura adequada, sem mobilidade, sem serviços públicos à altura das necessidades da população."

Ele também afirma que ainda existe um desafio relacionado à autoestima da população negra , construída historicamente sob condições de exclusão e discriminação.

"O povo negro ainda precisa elevar sua autoestima. Durante muito tempo foi levado a acreditar que não podia ocupar determinados espaços. Isso deixa marcas profundas", diz.

Para ele, o fortalecimento da identidade e o reconhecimento da contribuição histórica da população negra são fundamentais para mudar esse cenário.

Questionado sobre o legado que espera das próximas gerações, Côrtes responde sem falar de homenagens, monumentos ou títulos. O sonho é outro.

Ele gostaria que, no futuro, políticas criadas para combater desigualdades deixassem de ser necessárias porque o problema teria sido superado .

"Eu gostaria que não houvesse mais necessidade de cotas nem de ações afirmativas", confessa.

Faz questão, porém, de explicar o motivo: não porque essas políticas tenham perdido importância, mas porque espera que um dia elas tenham cumprido completamente sua missão:

"Que todos possam viver em paz, sem preconceito, sem racismo e sem segregação."

Dia da Consciência Negra será feriado nacional — Foto: Frederico Dávila/TV Globo

articles.title: Prazo para solicitar reaplicação do Enem 2026 termina hoje | G1
articles.standfirst: Quem estava doente ou foi prejudicado por problemas logísticos no local do exame, desde que comprovados, tem direito a fazer a '2ª chamada'. Inscrições vão até 20 de novembro.
articles.summary: Quem estava doente ou foi prejudicado por problemas logísticos no local do exame, desde que comprovados, tem direito a fazer a '2ª chamada'. Inscrições vão até 20 de novembro.
articles.body:
Os candidatos do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) 2026 que não compareceram a um dos domingos de provas, em 8 e 15 de novembro, por motivos de saúde ou problemas logísticos têm direito a participar da reaplicação do exame nos dias 15 e 16 de dezembro .

O prazo para solicitar a reaplicação termina nesta sexta-feira (20). Os candidatos afetados devem acessar a Página do Participante no prazo informado e apresentar documentos que comprovem o problema.

Participante de 39 locais ( 36 no RJ, dois no AP e um em MG ) terão direito à reaplicação após o MEC ter confirmado problemas de falta de energia nesses locais.

🚨 Mas atenção: em alguns casos, o aluno que faltou no primeiro dia (8) precisava comparecer ao segundo dia (15). Neste caso, ele não tem direito a refazer o exame nos dois dias e fará a prova em dezembro apenas referente ao dia em que se ausentou. (Entenda mais abaixo.)

Enem 2024 - Domingo (3) – Campinas (SP) – Últimos candidatos a entrar antes do fechamento dos portões — Foto: Pedro Amatuzzi/g1

Quem pode pedir para fazer a reaplicação?

Participantes afetados por erros na aplicação do exame ou por falta de energia elétrica no local de prova, enchentes e outros desastres naturais na região;

Candidatos que estavam com doenças infectocontagiosas (tuberculose, coqueluche, difteria, doença invasiva por Haemophilus influenzae, doença meningocócica e outras meningites, varíola, Mpox, influenza humana A e B, poliomielite por poliovírus selvagem, sarampo, rubéola, varicela (catapora) e covid-19).

Atenção: quem não conseguiu fazer a prova em um ou nos dois dias por falta opcional ou atraso não tem direito à reaplicação, a menos que o motivo seja comprovadamente associado a um dos motivos previstos em edital e descritos acima.

É preciso entrar na Página do Participante e inserir login e senha.

Entre 16 de 20 de novembro de 2026, o candidato poderá abrir o pedido de reaplicação para fazer o Enem em dezembro.

Se a justificativa for relacionada a problemas de saúde, será preciso anexar documentos comprobatórios (como exames e atestados médicos).

Nos casos de falhas logísticas, o próprio Inep irá analisar a situação do local de prova em que o participante estava inscrito.

Faltei no primeiro dia; devia ter feito a prova no segundo domingo, 15 de novembro?

Se o seu problema foi logístico, sim , você devia ter comparecido ao 2º domingo de Enem, em 15 de novembro , e fazer a reaplicação somente da 1ª etapa (em 15 de dezembro). Neste caso, a falta no segundo dia de provas é considerada opcional e não garante o direito à reaplicação da segunda prova.

Em caso de problemas de saúde , pode ficar tranquilo e se recuperar plenamente. Em dezembro, você fará os dois dias de Enem (15 e 16 de dezembro) , desde que sua solicitação seja aceita pelo Inep.

Passei mal durante a prova. Posso pedir reaplicação?

Não. Se você deixou o local de prova antes do horário permitido (15h30) em qualquer um dos dois dias, mesmo que tenha sido por problema de saúde, está eliminado do Enem 2026 e não tem direito de refazer a prova em dezembro.

Meu telefone tocou durante a prova. Posso pedir reaplicação?

Não. O edital prevê a eliminação do candidato cujo aparelho eletrônico (celular, relógio ou outro equipamento) toque ou receba notificações durante a prova, sem direito direito à reaplicação em dezembro.

articles.title: NI health: Resident doctors to begin 24-hour industrial action
articles.summary: A full 24-hour strike begins at 07:00 GMT - the second such action taken by doctors this year.
articles.body:
Resident doctors are set to return to the picket lines on Friday in a strike over pay.

They will hold a full 24-hour strike starting at 07:00 GMT, marking their second such action this year .

British Medical Association (BMA) members voted in favour of industrial action after the union rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise from an independent pay body.

Health Minister Robbie Butler said he remained committed to delivering the pay award and that he would "do everything in my power" to implement it this year - but said he was unable to do so in the absence of a Stormont budget .

Dr Steven Montgomery, the chairman of the BMA's Northern Ireland Resident Doctors Committee, said doctors should not have to strike for a second time but the issues that had originally taken them to the picket lines remained unresolved.

"Our pay is eroding and we need to address that in order to retain young doctors in Northern Ireland," he said.

Hospital doctors to strike as pay dispute continues

Health workers run out of patience with Stormont budget delay

Healthcare workers at 'tipping point' as union ballots for industrial action

Resident doctors are fully qualified medical practitioners who are completing postgraduate clinical training in a hospital or general practice under the supervision of a senior doctor.

Consultants and specialist, associate specialist and speciality grade (SAS) doctors will also take 24-hour action from 07:00 GMT on Monday.

They will provide what is known as Christmas Day cover, which means that most routine and elective services will be cancelled but full emergency cover will remain in place.

SAS doctors are specialist doctors employed by health trusts.

During this period of strike action more than 2,200 appointments were cancelled across the health and social care system, according to the health minister.

Butler said the fresh action planned for Friday and Monday would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery", especially during the busy winter period.

In England, consultant doctors have called off their two-day strike this month to hold talks with the government.

Montgomery said colleagues wanted the best for the health service and their patients but were facing burnout and emotional distress due to work pressure, with their pay failing to reflect the demands placed upon them.

He said doctors wanted full "pay restoration", adding that the annual pay rise they were due to receive would not make up for the value their pay had lost over many years.

Montgomery added that the BMA was "more than willing" to discuss with the minister and Department of Health how pay "erosion" could be addressed and what steps were needed to reassure members that there was a commitment to resolving it.

Butler said the recommended 3.5% rise was higher than that for other healthcare professionals working in Northern Ireland's health system.

He added that to go beyond the recommended offer would lead to "significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce".

"It comes on top of an average cumulative pay uplifts over the last three years of 30% for resident doctors, 25% for speciality, associate specialist, and specialist doctors, and 24% for consultants," he said.

The minister said he had met the BMA and outlined the financial constraints facing the Department of Health and his intention to issue the pay rises as soon as possible.

But he said that would require adequate funding to be given to his department.

images.caption: Hospital doctors also took strike action in June 2026

articles.title: Thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret operation
articles.summary: Supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and stadiums have been scrambling to make their devices safe.
articles.body:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies .

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.

They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.

"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.

There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:

In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted

On 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted

On 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium, Luxembourg the were worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted

The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).

RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.

As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.

These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.

"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.

RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.

The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.

"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.

RDM confirmed that there was no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continued to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers

If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

images.caption: Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature

articles.title: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
articles.summary: Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary is among the big investors looking to Canada as a data centre development destination, while his US project faces local opposition.
articles.body:
As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.

"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.

While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.

Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.

"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.

"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."

Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.

At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.

The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed".

One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah.

His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border.

Residents in Utah have organised a fierce opposition campaign. The pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Leary scale down the project by 75% , from 40,000 to 13,000 acres.

Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project.

The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality.

The project is billed as "off-grid" , relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta government exempted the project from an environmental impact assessment , arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction.

The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident, Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June that he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere".

In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years.

Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools.

Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks.

"It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place.

Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace.

He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months.

Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents.

"If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in an August town hall reported on by the Canadian Press , held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) AI data centre in the province.

Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings.

This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns.

There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.

On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered in Canada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre that will be used by technology giant Anthropic.

But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom.

"AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy.

"I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said.

So far, lawmakers in Canada have stood firm.

The Carney government, which has made reducing Canada's reliance on the US a priority, has framed the development of AI data centres as a matter of national security and sovereignty. It has projected that Canada needs to expand its computing capacity 16-fold over the next four years to meet domestic demand.

Alberta is defending its data centre plans by saying they will create jobs and generate revenue, and that sites will be developed "responsibly".

In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford has said that his province needs to move "full steam ahead" with building data centres.

Mullin said one reason the backlash had been less severe in Canada was simply due to scope and timing.

"There has been less of these projects happening, and as a result, they've attracted less attention," he said.

Canada has released some high-level guidance on data centre development, which has been co-signed by Anthropic, Meta and other big AI players. It calls on data centres to pay for electricity costs, minimise water use and create long-term benefits for the regions they are in.

If politicians don't tread carefully, Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who has fought a proposed hyperscale data centre in her community, said she believed public discontent could translate into angry votes, like those seen in the US.

MacIntosh successfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta, over concerns with its scale, scope and proximity to her home. Even after her eight-month battle, she said she was not opposed to all AI infrastructure and believed Canada had the resources and landscape to build them responsibly.

But she fears Alberta has opened the door to "the most reckless of reckless developers", and warned that voters might have a "knee-jerk reaction" if provinces don't take care to develop AI data centres responsibly.

"And I don't think any political party in Canada is prepared for it."

'We all need data, but do we need the largest data centre in Europe here?'

Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?

Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff

images.caption: Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary is behind a major AI data centre project in Canada that has so far been embraced by legislators.

articles.title: Hasan Piker complains the far left has less leverage with Democratic Party because the Dems won too many seats
articles.summary: Hasan Piker lamented Democrats' vast midterm margin weakened the far left's leverage, saying a smaller win could have allowed socialists to pressure the party.
articles.body: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker lamented that Democrats were so successful in the midterms they aren’t as dependent on their far-left flank. The Democrats won a resounding victory in the midterms, which surprised not only the Republican Party, but the far left. Just a month before the midterms, Piker had talked about using the far left to pressure candidate James Talarico to push progressive policy, saying, "We are the force that allowed him to win this seat of power, and if he wants to maintain it, he’s got to play ball." On Wednesday night, however, Piker played a different tune, noting that the Democratic Party was so successful it is no longer as dependent on support from its most left-wing members. HASAN PIKER DECLARES 'WOKE IS BACK,' FANTASIZES ABOUT PUTTING DONALD TRUMP IN PRISON "I think that there was a way that we could possibly get out of this fight with clear concessions on our agenda. We didn't. Part of that was because nobody expected the margin to be so vast," he said. "If the margin was 10, then we could have made an impact. If the Democratic Party's margin of victory was 10 and not like f---ing 40, OK, then yeah, we could have had a big caucus, a socialist caucus, a fighter caucus, whatever you want to call it, that could potentially bully the party to be more responsive to the needs of the masses." Piker also hit back at some critical comments from his fans. "’This is you at your worst,'" he read aloud one comment before responding. "Why? Because I have to explain to you as an adult who is a political pundit how, you know, how change never really happens in Washington, D.C.? "It hurts your feelings to hear someone explain to you why these things happen while simultaneously telling you how much I oppose it? Does it hurt your feelings to hear how this goes?" he asked. "It's just reality. "I'm going to continue to explain how the sausage gets made, even if that hurts your f---ing feelings, because you're too dumb to understand." Republican consultant Mary Marslender reacted to Piker's commentary. "Hasan Piker is furious that Democrats won too many seats because it weakened the (Democratic Socialists of America's) ability to hold the Democratic Party hostage. Piker’s complaint reveals that the far left prefers narrow majorities so it can force its destructive socialist experiments on our country and European-style street chaos," she told Fox News Digital. FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER GLOATS AFTER DEM BLOWOUT, PROMISES ‘JAIL’ FOR CONSERVATIVE ENEMIES Democratic strategist and co-host of "The Huddle" podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, "There is the world as Hasan Piker wished it would be, and the real world. Socialists are utterly irrelevant in the next Congress. They are not the majority of America, nor are they the majority of the Democratic Party. "In fact, in the next Congress, socialists will be a tiny 2.7% of the House Democratic caucus and there will be only one in the Senate, Bernie Sanders."
