articles.title: COP31: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
articles.summary: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
articles.body:
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.

A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.

"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.

"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."

Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.

Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.

In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.

Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.

"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.

He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.

"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.

After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.

"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."

A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.

"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.

The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.

The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.

But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.

He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.

Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.

"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.

'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted

Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.

The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.

Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.

Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.

Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.

But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?

"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.

"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."

Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.

"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.

She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.

"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.

"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."

African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.

"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.

"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."

The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.

Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.

"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.

But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.

"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.

Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.

In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.

UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.

But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.

Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.

"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.

"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

articles.title: US army warns detonation of unstable explosives will create toxic plume
articles.summary: The Army has delayed the controlled explosion of unstable lead azide in eastern Iowa to Monday after concerns from residents and lawmakers.
articles.body:
The US Army is set to detonate five tonnes of degraded explosive material in Middletown, Iowa, and have urged locals to vacate the area or stay indoors for their safety.

The detonations will result in an air plume that could send toxic dust, containing lead particles, over eastern Iowa and into neighbouring Illinois, with the potential for contaminants to settle on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, the army said.

The two controlled explosions will be powerful enough that they could damage buildings and shatter windows nearby.

On Thursday, environmental groups sued in an effort to stop the detonations, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives or give adequate notice.

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon local time (1800 BST) on Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown - a community of about 360 people about four hours west of Chicago, Illinois.

The plant produces medium- and large-calibre munitions for the US Department of Defense.

On Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle delayed the detonation to Monday, saying that "public safety is the Army's top priority".

The planned detonation will be "the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material", he said on X.

The army said that the detonation is part of "a planned and controlled safety operation" to dispose of degraded lead azide. It added that the detonation has been permitted by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under conservation and recovery laws.

Residents have been asked to leave their homes for about six hours - between 08:00 and 14:00 local time - while the operation takes place and the dust settles. The army said that "all humans" should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas.

Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise, feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations and will see a plume of dust, the advisory said.

According to Iowa Public Radio , the IAAAP found earlier this year that the lead azide - a highly volatile compound used as a detonator - stored in underground concrete tanks is degrading, becoming too unstable to safely move.

Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place is the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, said that the substance has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers.

It sits in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, but a routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati told the Associated Press.

The army said the lead azide barrels will be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with barriers full of sand. The soil above will be saturated with water in an effort to reduce the lead in the air.

On Thursday, two environmental groups sued to block the detonation, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal."

articles.title: A US woman spent years unaware that she had an older brother; the siblings, separated shortly after birth, finally found each other in their 80s after an ancestry test
articles.summary: Brother and sister separated by foster care shortly after birth found each other after almost 80 years apart when Marian Griffin, now 81, a California
articles.body: Brother and sister separated by foster care shortly after birth found each other after almost 80 years apart when Marian Griffin, now 81, a California woman, learned of an older brother, Donald Hefke, now 82, in 2024. Hefke’s family had spent decades trying to find her, while she had never known he existed. Griffin had always felt something was missing from her life, though she never knew what. Hefke’s daughter, Denise Baker, and an ancestry test completed by Griffin’s son made the reunion possible. Hefke was born in 1944, a year before Griffin, and a third sibling, Ernest, was born deaf and has since died.Why two Chicago babies ended up in foster care after their mother entered a mental institutionAccording to ABC News, the siblings were living with their birth parents when their mother, who had been struggling with post-traumatic stress disorder, was placed in a mental institution shortly after Griffin’s birth. Their father could not look after the children alone, and in 1946 they entered foster care, with Griffin just eight months old and Hefke barely over a year old, according to Baker. Griffin was adopted by a Lutheran minister and his family, while Hefke remained with a foster family until he was commissioned into the United States Air Force.The 1963 letter that revealed a sister named Marian, and the adoptive parents who hid his requestsHefke, determined to learn more about his biological family, contacted the foster care agency in 1963, and it replied with a little information, including that he had a sister named Marian. He then tried to reach Griffin’s adoptive parents, who told him to stop bothering them and hid his requests for contact from Griffin, even though she was already 18 and out of high school. Griffin told ABC News that if she had known, she would have looked for him and the two of them would have been together, and that their children could have grown up together instead of being kept apart.How more than two decades of paperwork and a son’s ancestry test finally led to Marian GriffinBaker took up the search as an adult and spent more than two decades going through paperwork, online research and ancestry websites. As 94.5 The Buzz reported, she finally succeeded in 2024, when she found that Griffin’s son had taken a genetic test through Ancestry.com. Seeing a connection, she contacted him, and he passed her details to Griffin in July 2024. Griffin’s first reaction was that it was a scam.From a first phone call to a planned reunion in FloridaAfter several conversations with Baker, Griffin spoke to her older brother for the first time, and she said he kept repeating her name and telling her he had found her. When the story was reported in July 2025, Griffin was 80 and Hefke 81. She lived in California and he, in poor health, in Florida, so they had celebrated by telephone, although Baker had travelled to California in June 2025 and saw in her aunt a strong likeness to her own father in looks, speech and manner. 94.5 The Buzz reported that Griffin planned to fly to Florida to see her brother soon, and she said they had 80 years of catching up to do. Her advice to others was not to give up on each other.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump vs New York Times: US judge allows $15 billion defamation lawsuit to move ahead
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House has cleared a key legal hurdle, with a
articles.body: US President Donald Trump’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House has cleared a key legal hurdle, with a federal judge in Florida allowing seven statements at the centre of the case to proceed while dismissing several other allegations.US district judge Steven D Merryday of the Middle District of Florida on Thursday rejected the defendants’ request to throw out the entire lawsuit.However, he dismissed 27 statements that Trump had identified as defamatory, ruling that they did not meet the high legal standard required for a public official to establish defamation.The decision leaves Trump free to pursue claims over seven statements harmed his reputation as a successful businessman and undermined his candidacy in the 2024 presidential election.Seven statements remain at the centre of Trump’s lawsuitOf the seven statements allowed to proceed, one appeared in an October 2024 article published by The New York Times, while the remaining six featured in the book Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success.The book was published by Penguin Random House and co-authored by Times reporters Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner. The lawsuit also names reporter Peter Baker.Trump has challenged statements concerning his role in creating his hit reality television show The Apprentice, the inheritance he received from his father, his business ventures and his upbringing in New York. His complaint initially cited 22 statements from a book by Baker and 12 from articles written by Craig and Buettner.The allegations that remain in the case centre on claims that Trump perpetrated or benefited from crimes, including tax evasion and money laundering. Merryday said Trump had plausibly argued that the seven statements were “based on incomplete, minimal information”.However, the judge dismissed every statement from a September 2024 article in The New York Times, along with several others from the October 2024 article and the book.Why the judge rejected most of the claimsMerryday ruled that 27 of the statements highlighted by Trump did not meet the high threshold a public official must cross to establish defamation.The Times and Penguin Random House had argued that the lawsuit was legally flawed and that Trump had failed to establish that the reporters acted with “actual malice”. The legal standard refers to knowingly publishing false information or doing so with reckless disregard for whether it was true.The publishers have denied defaming Trump and defended the accuracy of the reporting.The case has undergone several changes since it was first filed. Trump initially sued the publishers and the three journalists in September, last year, which was dismissed. He then filed an amended 40-page complaint in October, 2025, removing references to the 2024 presidential election. Efforts to resolve the dispute through mediation failed, while the defendants' request to transfer the case to federal court in New York was also unsuccessful.New York Times, Penguin Random House react to rulingThe New York Times welcomed the dismissal of most of the allegations but maintained that the remaining claims also lacked legal merit.“The Times is encouraged to see Judge Merryday’s dismissal of almost all claims against us,” Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesperson for the newspaper, said in a statement cited by NYT.“We continue to believe the remaining claim in the filing has no legal merit. We look forward to making this argument as we continue to defend ourselves against this baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country.”Penguin Random House also welcomed the dismissal of most of the case but said it was disappointed that some statements had been allowed to remain under consideration.The publisher said it was disappointed that the judge did not dismiss “several statements that have been widely reported for years and never challenged by President Trump, even in prior litigation.”“We are confident that the evidence in this case will lead to a full dismissal and continue to stand by the book and its authors,” the publisher said.The lawsuit is part of a series of legal actions Trump has pursued against media organisations during his second term.His $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal was dismissed with prejudice in October, preventing him from refiling the case, although he has appealed the decision. Separately, a federal judge earlier this month allowed Trump's lawsuit against the BBC to proceed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Indonesian daycare principal jailed for five years over child abuse case
articles.summary: Toddlers were found with their hands and feet tied with rags when police raided the centre in April.
articles.body:
The former principal of a daycare centre in Indonesia has been sentenced to five years in jail over the abuse and neglect of children in the unlicensed facility.

In April, a raid of the Little Aresha centre in the city of Yogyakarta exposed the culture of abuse within its walls – where toddlers were found with their hands and feet tied with rags .

The case sparked nationwide outrage and prompted further scrutiny of childcare centres across Indonesia, many of which authorities say are not properly licensed.

Little Aresha's principal, Anita Palupi Indahsari, was charged along with 11 staff members and the head of the foundation running the centre.

On Thursday, Yogyakarta judge Sunaryanto ruled that Anita had "allowed violence against children to be carried out continuously" and was "legally and convincingly guilty", according to AFP news agency.

The judge also ordered Anita to pay 510 million rupiah ($27,900; £21,300) in fines, failing which, her property will be seized and auctioned.

But some of the victims' families found the verdict - half of the ten-year jail term that prosecutors were initially arguing for - incommensurate with the traumatic impact their children had suffered.

Tri Susilawati, a parent present at Thursday's hearing, urged prosecutors to file an appeal, arguing that it was not adequate for "what they have done to our children".

Diyah Kusumastuti, the chairperson of the Little Aresha Foundation who was tried earlier in the year, had been sentenced to 10 years in prison.

The 11 caregivers employed by the centre were each handed jail terms ranging between two to three years – lower than the five-year terms prosecutors had sought.

The victims' families had protested against the earlier verdicts, with some saying the sentences were "far from what [they] had hoped for".

"It is very unfair," said Imedia Dwi Anjani, a victim's father.

The April raid at Little Aresha came after a former employee lodged a police report claiming that children had suffered inhumane treatment at the centre.

Police estimate that 53 out of the 103 children at the centre were mistreated. They also found as many as 20 children crammed into tiny rooms measuring about 3m (10ft) by 3m.

Yogyakarta's police chief Eva Guna Pandia said at the time that staff had tied some of the children up so they would not disturb others, AFP reported.

The centre was closed shortly after the raid.

articles.title: Amazon issues ‘another warning’ over New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s labor bill after threatening to pull 5,000 delivery jobs
articles.summary: Amazon has stepped up its campaign against a labor bill in New York City amid a growing talk that the City Council could vote on the pro-worker
articles.body: Amazon has stepped up its campaign against a labor bill in New York City amid a growing talk that the City Council could vote on the pro-worker legislation as early as next month. Amazon has reportedly begun speaking directly to its New York customers about the Delivery Protection Act, also known as Intro 518. Messages on its website and app warn shoppers they could be charged up to $5 more per order if the bill passes, as per a report by The New York Post.What the bill would doThe bill would end Amazon’s reliance on subcontractors and require it to hire its delivery workers directly. Other companies, including FedEx, would also have to follow the new rules. A super majority of council members, along with Mayor Zohran Mamdani, back the bill. They have been urging the Speaker to call a vote. Supporters, including the Teamsters, want the vote to happen before the end of the year.Is the direct-hire rule stayingIt is not clear whether the final bill will keep the direct-hire mandate, even though the Speaker has said publicly that she wants to protect jobs.“The concept that the direct-hire mandate is totally coming out is not true – the direct hire mandate is still on the table. That’s one of the core pieces that is being negotiated at this point,” a source close to the situation was quoted as saying. The same person added that a direct employment requirement is an unlikely outcome, but that no one has committed to removing it from the conversation.Amazon urges customers to contact lawmakersAmazon asked customers to get in touch with their City Council members. It gave them a form and a link to send messages saying they do not want “slower and more expensive” service. The company told The Post that about 20,000 New Yorkers clicked the link in the first six hours.Sources familiar with the matter say Amazon believes time is running out.“As the City Council continues to review this bill, we want to be transparent with our customers about what it would cost them if it passes as written – which is why we’re doing this,” Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement.Amazon’s pressure campaign so farThursday’s appeal is an escalation from Amazon’s earlier efforts, which include months of TV ads and rallies about the bill’s possible impact, the report said. One rally took place on Thursday outside the office of the bill’s sponsor, Tiffany Cabán (D-Queens). It was organised by New York Delivers, a coalition made up of Amazon subcontractors and others.The Seattle-based company again threatened to move its distribution centers outside the city. It says the bill would require it to hire 5,000 delivery workers who are currently employed by 40 subcontractors distributing packages in the city.According to previous US media reports, experts warn the standoff could lead Amazon to not only pull those 5,000 contracted delivery roles out of the city, but also shut all 15 of its last-mile fulfillment stations across New York City, eliminating the jobs of 2,000 internal warehouse workers who staff them.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Meta threatens to pull WhatsApp from Canada; tells government: Your demands ignore software realities
articles.summary: Meta has warned Canadian lawmakers that it may consider pulling encrypted services from the country if the federal government passes its proposed lawful
articles.body: Meta has warned Canadian lawmakers that it may consider pulling encrypted services from the country if the federal government passes its proposed lawful access legislation without further amendments. Speaking before a Senate committee reviewing Bill C-22, company representatives this week argued that the draft law would force technology companies to compromise digital security in order to comply with police warrants.Bill C-22, which passed the House of Commons in June, requires electronic service providers to adapt their systems so that they can hand over user data to investigators upon request. Critics say the mandate directly threatens end-to-end encryption, which is the security standard used by platforms like WhatsApp, Facebook, and Instagram to ensure messages can only be read by the sender and recipient."Ultimately, the Canadian government would be enforcing and imposing a law that it is not technically feasible to comply with and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services to Canadians," Robyn Greene, Meta’s director of privacy and public policy, testified before senators, according to a report in CBC.When pressed on whether the company would withdraw products from the Canadian market if the bill becomes law, Rachel Curran, Meta’s head of public policy for Canada, said the company would have to "review all of our options." Curran previously told Bloomberg that weakening encryption is a "red line" for Meta, warning the legislation risks turning private companies into "an arm of the government's surveillance apparatus."Why technology companies are upset with Bill C-22The standoff centers on Part 2 of Bill C-22, which grants ministers the authority to issue confidential orders compelling tech companies to build law enforcement access capabilities into their platforms. The provision also allows the government to require companies to retain customer metadata—including IP addresses and connection logs—for up to six months.While Ottawa introduced amendments barring orders that create a "systemic vulnerability," tech leaders and cybersecurity experts contend the language is overly vague. Cryptographers and privacy advocates have long maintained that it is impossible to build a "backdoor" exclusively for police without leaving that same entry point exposed to cybercriminals and foreign intelligence agencies.The primary flashpoint is Part 2 of the bill, which grants ministers in the country the authority to issue confidential orders forcing service providers to build interception capabilities for police. The legislation also empowers the government to require companies to retain sensitive customer metadata—including IP addresses and connection logs—for up to six months.While Ottawa introduced amendments prohibiting orders that create a "systemic vulnerability," tech leaders and cryptographers argue the language is dangerously vague. Security experts maintain that creating a "backdoor" for law enforcement inevitably creates a weak point that malicious hackers and foreign spies will eventually exploit.Meta is far from alone in its opposition, joining a broad coalition of tech giants, privacy-focused apps, and digital rights advocates pushing back against the draft law. Both Google and Apple have issued warnings that Bill C-22 threatens customer security and could break end-to-end encryption.Encrypted messaging platform Signal too has stated that it would leave Canada rather than compromise its security protocols, while Toronto-based VPN provider Windscribe pledged to maintain its strict no-logs policy regardless of the bill's outcome.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: US prosecutor declines charges against white cop who killed Black man
articles.summary: A police officer in the US state of Wisconsin, who fatally shot a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor
articles.body: A police officer in the US state of Wisconsin, who fatally shot a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor said on Thursday, ruling that the use of deadly force was justified.The decision drew sharp criticism from the victim's family and civil rights advocates.Dane County district attorney Ismael Ozanne said officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson acted reasonably when he shot Corey Ruiz on July 22. According to the prosecutor, Ruiz resisted officers, pulled out a knife and remained unaffected by multiple Taser rounds before the officer opened fire, Associated Press reported.Ozanne said the circumstances left the officer with no reasonable alternative and that there was no potential criminal liability. He said his decision followed a review of police reports, diagrams, surveillance footage, squad car videos and recordings made by members of the public. Madison police officers do not wear body cameras.The shooting was captured on video and had triggered racial justice protests and demands for police reform. Reacting to the decision, Ruiz's brother Adam accused the prosecutor of mistreating the family.“We’re destroyed,” he told reporters. “We won’t accept this.”Family attorney challenges prosecutor's findingsCivil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the Ruiz family, said the videos did not justify the shooting and described the incident as one of the worst cases of excessive force he had handled, AP reported.“In the video you see they tackle him, they tase him, they kick him and then the police officer executes him,” Crump said at a news conference alongside the family. “The video is the objective unbiased witness here.”Crump said Baitinger-Peterson fired three shots at Ruiz while he was on the ground, with two hitting his chest and the third striking his head. He said the medical examiner had told the family that Ruiz would have survived if the third shot had not been fired.Defending his decision, Ozanne said he had applied the law to the facts of the case.“A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law; however, I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand,” he said. “The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not.”What happened during the shootingBaitinger-Peterson was among four officers who responded to reports of a person checking parked cars and an alleged attempted burglary on July 22, police said. They found Ruiz on a bicycle and surrounded him at an intersection, where a struggle followed.Dash-camera footage released by the Wisconsin department of justice on Thursday shows officers repeatedly shouting, “He’s got a knife! He’s got a knife!” Ruiz is seen holding a knife in his right hand, with the blade pointing downwards.As a fourth officer arrived and deployed a Taser, Ruiz stumbled and fell on his right side. Baitinger-Peterson then fired three shots at close range.In an interview with investigators days after the shooting, the officer said he had knelt down and grabbed Ruiz's right arm before realising he was holding a knife. He said he struggled to control the arm and feared Ruiz would stab the officers.Baitinger-Peterson also told investigators that he fired the third shot because Ruiz's facial expression and body did not change after the first two shots, leading him to believe they had not hit him.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Florida carried out its 20th execution of the year on Thursday after putting to death a 71-year-old man convicted of murdering a pregnant woman, her
articles.body: Florida carried out its 20th execution of the year on Thursday after putting to death a 71-year-old man convicted of murdering a pregnant woman, her husband and their unborn child during a 1991 home invasion in the Florida Keys.Thomas Mitchell Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 pm EST following a three-drug lethal injection at Florida State Prison. However, he denied the allegations."I've never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone," Overton said in his final statement. "I didn't kill the MacIvors."Pregnant woman, husband strangled in 1991 home invasionThe bodies of Michael and Susan MacIvor were discovered at their home in Tavernier, Florida, on August 22, 1991. Court records showed that both had been strangled, while an autopsy found that Susan, who was eight months pregnant, had been raped.The medical examiner concluded that the couple's unborn son likely survived for around half an hour after his mother's death.Investigators collected DNA evidence from the crime scene but initially found no match in the state's database. Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the couple's home, was arrested in 1996 in connection with an unrelated burglary. His DNA sample subsequently matched evidence recovered from the MacIvors' home.He was convicted in 1999 on two counts of first-degree murder and received a death sentence for each killing.With Overton's execution, Florida accounted for more than half of the 39 executions carried out across the United States so far this year, AP reports.Florida is scheduled to carry out two more executions in December, which could further raise its annual tally.You use AI every day. articles.body: Fiona, the hippopotamus whose premature birth at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 made her a global sensation, has died aged nine after swallowing a visitor’s knit hat that accidentally landed in her enclosure. The zoo said Thursday that she died despite repeated attempts by veterinarians and keepers to treat the resulting medical emergency.“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo said in a statement.Fiona swallowed the hat about 11 days ago after a visitor tossed it into the air. A ceiling fan caught the object and deflected it through a small opening above the enclosure’s viewing windows, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley said. Curley described the incident as an accident.The zoo had been providing Fiona with round-the-clock care, keeping her hydrated, offering treats and monitoring her condition. Specialists advised that surgery was not an option for a full-grown hippo, the zoo said.The veterinary team also borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, hoping that the movement would help the hat pass through Fiona’s digestive tract. She was encouraged to stand on it several times a day.“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome,” the zoo said.Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated Fiona twice to assess her condition. An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines. A colonoscopy using a 9-foot (2.7-metre) scope did not locate the hat, he said.Fiona’s death prompted an immediate outpouring of grief. Visitors began leaving flowers and cards beside a hippo statue outside the zoo within an hour of the announcement. One note read, “Forever our Fiona.”Accorfing to news agency AP, Cincinnati mayor Aftab Pureval called Fiona “a symbol of perseverance and joy”, while Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine described her as “a true icon”. The Cincinnati Bengals also paid tribute, calling her “the queen of the Queen City”.Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), and initially struggled to stand and nurse.
